blocks.text: Huygens' principle, first stated by the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens, is a geometrical method for finding the shape of a wavefront at a later time from its known shape at some instant. Huygens assumed that every point of a wavefront can be considered a source of secondary wavelets that spread out in all directions with a speed equal to the speed of the wave. The new wavefront at a later time is the surface tangent to all the secondary wavelets, called their envelope.

In Fig 15.2 the wavefront AB moves outward from a source S. To find its shape after a time t, assume the wave speed v is the same everywhere, so in time t the wave travels a distance vt. Draw circles (traces of spherical wavelets) of radius vt centred on points along AB. The envelope of these wavelets, the curve CD, is the new wavefront. All the results of Huygens' principle can also be obtained from Maxwell's equations, but Huygens' simple model is easier to use.

blocks.alt: A source S on the left and, to its right, a curved primary wavefront AB with seven points on it. From each point a secondary wavelet of radius vt is drawn; a pink line marks one radius and an arrow labelled vt shows the direction of travel. The curve CD touching all the wavelets is labelled secondary wavefront; one small arc is labelled wavelet.
